2.text: and tied to the hoop, near the handle. When thus taken apart, the drum

3.text: is put away in the family bag. It is but little work to soak the drum-head

4.text: and fasten it on, so that this is not done until just before the drum is wanted.

5.text: During the season of ceremonials the drum is hung on the frame of the outer

6.text: tent, ready for use. It is placed near the fire-board, because it plays an

8.text: With the Kolyma Chukchee the drum is considered of less importance

9.text: than the fire-board and charm-string. On the Pacific side the reverse is true.

10.text: There the drum is called the “voice of the hearth,” and it is more difficult

11.text: to obtain a drum which has been in use than to get a fire-board.

12.text: In the Kolyma and Anadyr countries, drums belonging to strange fami-

13.text: lies may be brought at least into the outer tent, and there played upon. At

14.text: the season of great ceremonials, as many as ten drums are sometimes beaten

15.text: at once in the same tent.

16.text: House. — The covering of the house and the sleeping-room, the poles

17.text: of the frame, the bedding and the pillow-bags, and the sledges on which

18.text: these things are carried, — all are considered to belong to the hearth. They

19.text: pass on to the heirs with the fire-boards and charm-strings, and with the lat-

20.text: ter are divided among the relatives.

21.text: When building a new tent, one man goes out into the woods and cuts

22.text: the three principal poles. After fastening them together and bringing them

23.text: home, he kills a reindeer and smears the poles with the blood of the sacri-

24.text: fice. Every year the poles receive a further sacrifice in midsummer, as will

26.text: The house with its belongings, the hearth with the fire-tools, and other

27.text: sacred objects, are thus all regarded as a unit. It is not very sinful to part

28.text: with some of these things (the Chukchee will sell, for example, a part of the

29.text: tent-covering to the Russians, or even give away charm-strings to the spirits);

30.text: but it is unpardonable to take any part of the home unit belonging to a

31.text: stranger, and use it in one’s own house. For this reason, though I was able

32.text: to procure (but not without some difficulty) a few fire-tools and charm-strings,

33.text: on bringing them into the tent which was my shelter for the night, I inva-

34.text: riably had trouble with the Chukchee tent-owners, who were unwilling to

35.text: have alien sacred things enter their dwelling. This peculiarity sometimes led

36.text: to disagreeable consequences, as, for instance, in the episode described on p. 38.

37.text: Sledges, however, may be used, provided they are not taken into the

38.text: tent. If a tent-pole which some one has lost on the road is found, it may

39.text: be used for fuel. No other part of the home unit can be used in any way.

40.text: If a house is left without a male heir, nobody will touch it, and it is left to

41.text: rot on the spot where it stands.
